content: 1. Clinical guidelines should be formulated with a focus on health technology assessment (HTA) tailored to the specific needs of different countries and health systems. For fragile states, essential services, emergency kits, and disaster planning must be defined. In low-income countries with low health coverage, primary healthcare packages should be established. For middle-income countries with low coverage, guaranteed packages of care should be defined. In strong health systems, marginal analysis should be used to evaluate additions to existing care packages. 2. All providers of palliative care, regardless of the care setting, must commit to the continuous improvement of service quality. Data collected from quality indicators serve as a primary source of information for enhancing these services. 3. A basic framework for indicators to assess key domains of national or regional palliative care programs is essential. Sample indicators include the existence of a national palliative care policy ensuring access to care and pain control with opioid medications, and the inclusion of palliative care in universal health coverage. 4. Laws and regulations must ensure the safe and effective prescribing of opioids in alignment with international drug conventions, both at the district and community levels. 5. The proportion of medical, nursing, and technical schools that include palliative care education in their undergraduate curricula should be monitored to ensure adequate training of healthcare professionals. 6. Palliative care must be included in the list of services provided at the primary care level. The proportion of communities offering palliative care services should also be tracked. 7. The availability of essential palliative care medicines, such as oral morphine, should be ensured at the district level, with stock availability monitored in at least one pharmacy per district. 8. Outcomes such as the percentage of patients with access to palliative care at the time of death and the number of patients receiving palliative care per 100,000 inhabitants should be measured. 9. Standard health metrics like quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) do not fully capture the objectives of health systems, such as alleviating patient suffering and providing financial risk protection. New research concepts, such as extended cost-effectiveness analysis (ECEA) and suffering-adjusted life years (SALYs), have been proposed to address these gaps. 10. The knowledge and attitudes of primary healthcare providers and community health workers (CHWs) regarding palliative care should be explored. This includes their ability to identify palliative care needs early in the course of life-limiting illnesses and their self-assessment of competencies in addressing social, spiritual, and legal issues. 11. Understanding the knowledge and attitudes of primary care providers about advance care planning can yield culturally specific insights. Similarly, studying the palliative care-related knowledge and attitudes of CHWs can help refine their training and support systems. 12. Integrating palliative care and symptom relief into primary healthcare requires a comprehensive approach, including policy development, education, service provision, and the availability of essential medicines.
